name: Alternaria Leaf Spot
description: If leaves, stems, or fruit suddenly look spotted, sunken, or rotting, alternaria leaf spot may already be active. This problem often starts small, then spreads across healthy tissue before most growers realize how serious it is. Warmth, moisture, and crowded foliage usually speed it up. Treat early, because waiting even a few days can turn a manageable infection into major crop loss.
characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. Check both leaf surfaces, stem bases, and fruit scars where symptoms first appear. New lesions after rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew are a strong clue. When separate spots begin merging into larger dead patches, the disease is advancing quickly.

control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. Keep flowering strips with dill, yarrow, alyssum, and cilantro nearby so hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoids stay active against the insects that open infection wounds. Add microbial inoculants like Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma at first symptom, then wait 48 hours before layering more treatments so you can see whether biology is already reducing new lesions.
control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Thin crowded canopies, prune crossing branches, and space replacements so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Rotate susceptible crops for at least one season and avoid planting the same host family back-to-back, because many disease organisms survive in debris and splash back onto new growth.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. For low-level pressure, strip isolated lesions and improve airflow; for fast-moving lesions on multiple plants, mechanical removal alone is not enough. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

name: Andean Potato Weevil
description: If plants are wilting, notching at the edges, or fruit and roots show hidden feeding damage, andean potato weevil may be the cause. Adults chew above ground while larvae often feed out of sight inside soil, stems, or fruit. Damage builds quietly, then plants crash fast when roots are heavily hit. Act early so a small weevil problem does not become a season-long infestation.
characteristics: Look for small beetles with a hard body and a distinct snout, usually active at dawn, dusk, or night. Check for crescent-shaped leaf notches, punctures in fruit, or tiny entry holes near stems. In soil or damaged tissue, larvae are often pale, legless, and curved in a C-shape. Fresh chew marks plus snout beetles or C-shaped grubs confirm active weevil pressure.

control_methods.biological_controls: Pause for 48 hours after first detection and scout for local helpers before spraying: lady beetle larvae, lacewings, minute pirate bugs, predatory mites, and parasitoid wasps often arrive quickly when nectar plants are nearby. Build that support system with dill, fennel, alyssum, cilantro, and yarrow around the bed edges so beneficials stay on site. Avoid buying bulk beneficial insects unless monitoring shows a true gap, because many purchased releases disperse fast and rarely match local timing.
control_methods.preventive_methods: Andean Potato Weevil pressure rises fastest on stressed plants with dense, humid canopies and frequent flushes of soft growth from overfeeding nitrogen. Keep fertility moderate, inspect new growth and leaf undersides weekly, and act when you see the first cluster instead of waiting for visible plant decline. Early warning signs include stippling, curled tips, sticky residue, frass, webbing, eggs, or small feeding scars around tender tissue.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Break the life cycle by removing heavily infested plant parts first, then reduce shelter with better spacing, strategic pruning, and cleanup of weeds or crop residue that can host carryover stages. Use companion strips such as garlic, chives, basil, marigold, nasturtium, or calendula to disrupt host-finding and concentrate pests where scouting is easier. Recheck in 3-4 days, because many warm-weather pest cycles can go from egg to reproducing adult in about a week.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Start with a strong water spray on leaf undersides or stems to dislodge soft-bodied stages, and hand-remove egg masses, rolled leaves, or bored tissue into soapy water. Add yellow or blue sticky cards at canopy height to track adult flights and verify whether pressure is dropping. If counts keep rising after two mechanical passes in one week, escalate quickly rather than repeating labor that no longer changes population trend.
control_methods.organic_sprays: For contact control, mix insecticidal soap at 1-2 teaspoons pure castile soap per quart of water and spray directly on pests, especially undersides and hidden clusters. Neem oil can be layered as a growth regulator at about 1 tablespoon neem plus 1 teaspoon soap per quart, applied at dusk every 3-7 days based on pressure. These sprays are non-selective on soft-bodied insects, so avoid open flowers, avoid spraying when beneficials are active, and expect suppression through repeated coverage rather than instant eradication.

Young stages are easy to miss, then damage suddenly explodes as they grow. Catch them early to avoid severe defoliation and contaminated harvests.
characteristics: Check leaf undersides, growing tips, and stem junctions for eggs, frass pellets, and feeding scars. Larvae vary in color, but most have a soft segmented body and blend into foliage. Look at dusk or early morning when many species feed more actively. Fresh chewing plus live larvae or droppings on lower leaves confirms an active caterpillar outbreak.

control_methods.biological_controls: Pause for 48 hours after first detection and scout for local helpers before spraying: lady beetle larvae, lacewings, minute pirate bugs, predatory mites, and parasitoid wasps often arrive quickly when nectar plants are nearby. Build that support system with dill, fennel, alyssum, cilantro, and yarrow around the bed edges so beneficials stay on site. Avoid buying bulk beneficial insects unless monitoring shows a true gap, because many purchased releases disperse fast and rarely match local timing.
control_methods.preventive_methods: Bagworm pressure rises fastest on stressed plants with dense, humid canopies and frequent flushes of soft growth from overfeeding nitrogen. Keep fertility moderate, inspect new growth and leaf undersides weekly, and act when you see the first cluster instead of waiting for visible plant decline. Early warning signs include stippling, curled tips, sticky residue, frass, webbing, eggs, or small feeding scars around tender tissue.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Break the life cycle by removing heavily infested plant parts first, then reduce shelter with better spacing, strategic pruning, and cleanup of weeds or crop residue that can host carryover stages. Use companion strips such as garlic, chives, basil, marigold, nasturtium, or calendula to disrupt host-finding and concentrate pests where scouting is easier. Recheck in 3-4 days, because many warm-weather pest cycles can go from egg to reproducing adult in about a week.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Start with a strong water spray on leaf undersides or stems to dislodge soft-bodied stages, and hand-remove egg masses, rolled leaves, or bored tissue into soapy water. Add yellow or blue sticky cards at canopy height to track adult flights and verify whether pressure is dropping. If counts keep rising after two mechanical passes in one week, escalate quickly rather than repeating labor that no longer changes population trend.
control_methods.organic_sprays: For contact control, mix insecticidal soap at 1-2 teaspoons pure castile soap per quart of water and spray directly on pests, especially undersides and hidden clusters. Neem oil can be layered as a growth regulator at about 1 tablespoon neem plus 1 teaspoon soap per quart, applied at dusk every 3-7 days based on pressure. These sprays are non-selective on soft-bodied insects, so avoid open flowers, avoid spraying when beneficials are active, and expect suppression through repeated coverage rather than instant eradication.

name: Brown Rot
description: If leaves, stems, or fruit suddenly look spotted, sunken, or rotting, brown rot may already be active. This problem often starts small, then spreads across healthy tissue before most growers realize how serious it is. Warmth, moisture, and crowded foliage usually speed it up. Treat early, because waiting even a few days can turn a manageable infection into major crop loss.
characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. Check both leaf surfaces, stem bases, and fruit scars where symptoms first appear. New lesions after rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew are a strong clue. When separate spots begin merging into larger dead patches, the disease is advancing quickly.

control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. Keep flowering strips with dill, yarrow, alyssum, and cilantro nearby so hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoids stay active against the insects that open infection wounds. Add microbial inoculants like Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma at first symptom, then wait 48 hours before layering more treatments so you can see whether biology is already reducing new lesions.
control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Thin crowded canopies, prune crossing branches, and space replacements so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Rotate susceptible crops for at least one season and avoid planting the same host family back-to-back, because many disease organisms survive in debris and splash back onto new growth.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. For low-level pressure, strip isolated lesions and improve airflow; for fast-moving lesions on multiple plants, mechanical removal alone is not enough. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

name: Carrot Fly
description: If leaves, stems, or fruit suddenly look spotted, sunken, or rotting, carrot fly may already be active. This problem often starts small, then spreads across healthy tissue before most growers realize how serious it is. Warmth, moisture, and crowded foliage usually speed it up. Treat early, because waiting even a few days can turn a manageable infection into major crop loss.
characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. Check both leaf surfaces, stem bases, and fruit scars where symptoms first appear. New lesions after rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew are a strong clue. When separate spots begin merging into larger dead patches, the disease is advancing quickly.

control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. Keep flowering strips with dill, yarrow, alyssum, and cilantro nearby so hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoids stay active against the insects that open infection wounds. Add microbial inoculants like Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma at first symptom, then wait 48 hours before layering more treatments so you can see whether biology is already reducing new lesions.
control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Thin crowded canopies, prune crossing branches, and space replacements so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Rotate susceptible crops for at least one season and avoid planting the same host family back-to-back, because many disease organisms survive in debris and splash back onto new growth.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. For low-level pressure, strip isolated lesions and improve airflow; for fast-moving lesions on multiple plants, mechanical removal alone is not enough. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

Early warning signs include stippling, curled tips, sticky residue, frass, webbing, eggs, or small feeding scars around tender tissue.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Break the life cycle by removing heavily infested plant parts first, then reduce shelter with better spacing, strategic pruning, and cleanup of weeds or crop residue that can host carryover stages. Use companion strips such as garlic, chives, basil, marigold, nasturtium, or calendula to disrupt host-finding and concentrate pests where scouting is easier. Recheck in 3-4 days, because many warm-weather pest cycles can go from egg to reproducing adult in about a week.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Start with a strong water spray on leaf undersides or stems to dislodge soft-bodied stages, and hand-remove egg masses, rolled leaves, or bored tissue into soapy water. Add yellow or blue sticky cards at canopy height to track adult flights and verify whether pressure is dropping. If counts keep rising after two mechanical passes in one week, escalate quickly rather than repeating labor that no longer changes population trend.
control_methods.organic_sprays: For contact control, mix insecticidal soap at 1-2 teaspoons pure castile soap per quart of water and spray directly on pests, especially undersides and hidden clusters. Neem oil can be layered as a growth regulator at about 1 tablespoon neem plus 1 teaspoon soap per quart, applied at dusk every 3-7 days based on pressure. These sprays are non-selective on soft-bodied insects, so avoid open flowers, avoid spraying when beneficials are active, and expect suppression through repeated coverage rather than instant eradication.

name: Cytospora Canker
description: If leaves, stems, or fruit suddenly look spotted, sunken, or rotting, cytospora canker may already be active. This problem often starts small, then spreads across healthy tissue before most growers realize how serious it is. Warmth, moisture, and crowded foliage usually speed it up. Treat early, because waiting even a few days can turn a manageable infection into major crop loss.
characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. Check both leaf surfaces, stem bases, and fruit scars where symptoms first appear. New lesions after rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew are a strong clue. When separate spots begin merging into larger dead patches, the disease is advancing quickly.

control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. Keep flowering strips with dill, yarrow, alyssum, and cilantro nearby so hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoids stay active against the insects that open infection wounds. Add microbial inoculants like Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma at first symptom, then wait 48 hours before layering more treatments so you can see whether biology is already reducing new lesions.
control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Thin crowded canopies, prune crossing branches, and space replacements so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Rotate susceptible crops for at least one season and avoid planting the same host family back-to-back, because many disease organisms survive in debris and splash back onto new growth.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. For low-level pressure, strip isolated lesions and improve airflow; for fast-moving lesions on multiple plants, mechanical removal alone is not enough. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

name: Heart Rot
scientific_name: Ganoderma zonatum (palms); other wood-decay basidiomycetes on trees
description: If leaves, stems, or fruit suddenly look spotted, sunken, or rotting, heart rot may already be active. This problem often starts small, then spreads across healthy tissue before most growers realize how serious it is. Warmth, moisture, and crowded foliage usually speed it up. characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. Check both leaf surfaces, stem bases, and fruit scars where symptoms first appear. New lesions after rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew are a strong clue. When separate spots begin merging into larger dead patches, the disease is advancing quickly.

control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. Keep flowering strips with dill, yarrow, alyssum, and cilantro nearby so hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoids stay active against the insects that open infection wounds. Add microbial inoculants like Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma at first symptom, then wait 48 hours before layering more treatments so you can see whether biology is already reducing new lesions.
control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Thin crowded canopies, prune crossing branches, and space replacements so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Rotate susceptible crops for at least one season and avoid planting the same host family back-to-back, because many disease organisms survive in debris and splash back onto new growth.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

control_methods.mechanical_physical: Start with a strong water spray on leaf undersides or stems to dislodge soft-bodied stages, and hand-remove egg masses, rolled leaves, or bored tissue into soapy water. Early warning signs include stippling, curled tips, sticky residue, frass, webbing, eggs, or small feeding scars around tender tissue.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Break the life cycle by removing heavily infested plant parts first, then reduce shelter with better spacing, strategic pruning, and cleanup of weeds or crop residue that can host carryover stages. Use companion strips such as garlic, chives, basil, marigold, nasturtium, or calendula to disrupt host-finding and concentrate pests where scouting is easier. Recheck in 3-4 days, because many warm-weather pest cycles can go from egg to reproducing adult in about a week.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Start with a strong water spray on leaf undersides or stems to dislodge soft-bodied stages, and hand-remove egg masses, rolled leaves, or bored tissue into soapy water. Add yellow or blue sticky cards at canopy height to track adult flights and verify whether pressure is dropping. If counts keep rising after two mechanical passes in one week, escalate quickly rather than repeating labor that no longer changes population trend.
control_methods.organic_sprays: For contact control, mix insecticidal soap at 1-2 teaspoons pure castile soap per quart of water and spray directly on pests, especially undersides and hidden clusters. Neem oil can be layered as a growth regulator at about 1 tablespoon neem plus 1 teaspoon soap per quart, applied at dusk every 3-7 days based on pressure. These sprays are non-selective on soft-bodied insects, so avoid open flowers, avoid spraying when beneficials are active, and expect suppression through repeated coverage rather than instant eradication.

name: Mealybugs
description: If new growth is curling, yellowing, sticky, or chewed, mealybugs may already be on the plant. This pest often builds quietly, then damage appears all at once. characteristics: Inspect the newest growth first: leaf undersides, flower buds, stem joints, and tender tips where pests gather. Matching visible pests with fresh plant damage confirms active infestation.

Affected plants often appear in patches rather than uniformly across the bed. Symptoms can mimic nutrient stress, but damaged roots with poor feeder growth are a key clue. Lab or microscope confirmation is best, but root injury patterns strongly indicate nematode pressure.

description: If plants are wilting, notching at the edges, or fruit and roots show hidden feeding damage, palm weevil may be the cause. Adults chew above ground while larvae often feed out of sight inside soil, stems, or fruit. Damage builds quietly, then plants crash fast when roots are heavily hit. Act early so a small weevil problem does not become a season-long infestation.

Check for crescent-shaped leaf notches, punctures in fruit, or tiny entry holes near stems. In soil or damaged tissue, larvae are often pale, legless, and curved in a C-shape. characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. name: Rice Blast Fungus
description: If leaves, stems, or fruit suddenly look spotted, sunken, or rotting, rice blast fungus may already be active. characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. Keep flowering strips with dill, yarrow, alyssum, and cilantro nearby so hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoids stay active against the insects that open infection wounds. control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Thin crowded canopies, prune crossing branches, and space replacements so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Rotate susceptible crops for at least one season and avoid planting the same host family back-to-back, because many disease organisms survive in debris and splash back onto new growth.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. For low-level pressure, strip isolated lesions and improve airflow; for fast-moving lesions on multiple plants, mechanical removal alone is not enough. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

name: Spotted Cucumber Beetle
description: If leaves, stems, or fruit suddenly look spotted, sunken, or rotting, spotted cucumber beetle may already be active. This problem often starts small, then spreads across healthy tissue before most growers realize how serious it is. Warmth, moisture, and crowded foliage usually speed it up. Treat early, because waiting even a few days can turn a manageable infection into major crop loss.
characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. Check both leaf surfaces, stem bases, and fruit scars where symptoms first appear. New lesions after rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew are a strong clue. When separate spots begin merging into larger dead patches, the disease is advancing quickly.

control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. Keep flowering strips with dill, yarrow, alyssum, and cilantro nearby so hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoids stay active against the insects that open infection wounds. Add microbial inoculants like Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma at first symptom, then wait 48 hours before layering more treatments so you can see whether biology is already reducing new lesions.
control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Thin crowded canopies, prune crossing branches, and space replacements so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Rotate susceptible crops for at least one season and avoid planting the same host family back-to-back, because many disease organisms survive in debris and splash back onto new growth.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. For low-level pressure, strip isolated lesions and improve airflow; for fast-moving lesions on multiple plants, mechanical removal alone is not enough. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

name: White Rot
description: If leaves, stems, or fruit suddenly look spotted, sunken, or rotting, white rot may already be active. This problem often starts small, then spreads across healthy tissue before most growers realize how serious it is. Warmth, moisture, and crowded foliage usually speed it up. Treat early, because waiting even a few days can turn a manageable infection into major crop loss.
characteristics: Look for a pattern, not one bad leaf: expanding spots, dark or pale halos, fuzzy growth, or tissue that collapses when touched. Check both leaf surfaces, stem bases, and fruit scars where symptoms first appear. New lesions after rain, overhead watering, or heavy dew are a strong clue. When separate spots begin merging into larger dead patches, the disease is advancing quickly.

control_methods.biological_controls: Start by protecting leaf-surface microbes and predators that naturally suppress disease spread. Keep flowering strips with dill, yarrow, alyssum, and cilantro nearby so hoverflies, lacewings, and parasitoids stay active against the insects that open infection wounds. Add microbial inoculants like Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma at first symptom, then wait 48 hours before layering more treatments so you can see whether biology is already reducing new lesions.
control_methods.preventive_methods: This problem usually explodes when leaves stay wet for long periods, airflow is poor, and plants are pushed with excess nitrogen into soft growth that infects easily. Water the soil early in the day, not the foliage at night, and keep mulch from touching stems so humidity does not sit on tissue. Treat the first two to three spots as an outbreak warning, because spores or bacteria can cycle fast and turn one patch into field-wide infection in under a week.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Remove the worst infected leaves first and bag them immediately so you are not shaking spores across healthy plants. Thin crowded canopies, prune crossing branches, and space replacements so leaves dry quickly after rain or dew. Rotate susceptible crops for at least one season and avoid planting the same host family back-to-back, because many disease organisms survive in debris and splash back onto new growth.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Prune at least 6 inches below visible symptoms with clean tools, then disinfect blades between cuts so you do not spread infection plant to plant. For low-level pressure, strip isolated lesions and improve airflow; for fast-moving lesions on multiple plants, mechanical removal alone is not enough. Escalate to targeted organic sprays when new spots keep appearing after two cleanup rounds within the same week.
control_methods.organic_sprays: Use potassium bicarbonate at 1 tablespoon per gallon as a knockdown spray, or wettable sulfur where label-safe, and cover both leaf surfaces until just before runoff. Apply at dusk or early morning when sun is mild, then repeat every 5-7 days while new symptoms appear. Do not spray oils within two weeks of sulfur, and keep sprays off open flowers and active beneficial-insect habitat because repeated broad coverage can disrupt pollinators and microbial balance.

Keep fertility moderate, inspect new growth and leaf undersides weekly, and act when you see the first cluster instead of waiting for visible plant decline. Early warning signs include stippling, curled tips, sticky residue, frass, webbing, eggs, or small feeding scars around tender tissue.
control_methods.cultural_practices: Break the life cycle by removing heavily infested plant parts first, then reduce shelter with better spacing, strategic pruning, and cleanup of weeds or crop residue that can host carryover stages. Use companion strips such as garlic, chives, basil, marigold, nasturtium, or calendula to disrupt host-finding and concentrate pests where scouting is easier. Recheck in 3-4 days, because many warm-weather pest cycles can go from egg to reproducing adult in about a week.
control_methods.mechanical_physical: Start with a strong water spray on leaf undersides or stems to dislodge soft-bodied stages, and hand-remove egg masses, rolled leaves, or bored tissue into soapy water. Add yellow or blue sticky cards at canopy height to track adult flights and verify whether pressure is dropping. If counts keep rising after two mechanical passes in one week, escalate quickly rather than repeating labor that no longer changes population trend.
control_methods.organic_sprays: For contact control, mix insecticidal soap at 1-2 teaspoons pure castile soap per quart of water and spray directly on pests, especially undersides and hidden clusters. Neem oil can be layered as a growth regulator at about 1 tablespoon neem plus 1 teaspoon soap per quart, applied at dusk every 3-7 days based on pressure. These sprays are non-selective on soft-bodied insects, so avoid open flowers, avoid spraying when beneficials are active, and expect suppression through repeated coverage rather than instant eradication.
